definitions.definition: When things fit together in an orderly, connected way, like a well-organized team working smoothly.
definitions.example: A perfectly tuned guitar string produces a coherent sound wave.

definitions.definition: The idea that the universe itself might have a built-in pattern or purpose, like a mind behind everything.
definitions.example: Some people think the laws of physics are so precise that they look like they were designed by a cosmic intelligence.

definitions.definition: A set of equations and rules used to describe how something works, like a recipe for reality.
definitions.example: Newton's laws of motion are a mathematical framework for predicting how a ball will roll.

definitions.definition: A perfect match in structure between two different things, like two puzzles that fit together the same way even though the pictures are different.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines because the connections match.

definitions.definition: A statement that has been proven true using logic and math, like a fact that can't be argued.
definitions.example: The Pythagorean theorem says that in a right triangle, a² + b² = c².

definitions.definition: A computer program that checks if a mathematical proof is correct, like a spell-checker for logic.
definitions.example: Lean 4 is a proof assistant that makes sure every step of a proof follows the rules.

definitions.definition: When the order of operations matters, like putting on socks then shoes vs. shoes then socks.
definitions.example: In math, subtraction is non-commutative because 5 - 3 is not the same as 3 - 5.

definitions.definition: A pattern made of three parts that work together, like a three-legged stool.
definitions.example: The Christian Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is a triadic structure.

definitions.definition: A free gift of love or help that you don't have to earn, like a surprise birthday present.
definitions.example: In Christianity, grace is God's unearned kindness toward people.

definitions.definition: When two statements cannot both be true at the same time, like saying 'it is raining' and 'it is not raining' at once.
definitions.example: If you say 'I am asleep' while talking, that's a contradiction.

definitions.definition: A basic math fact that zero does not equal one, used as a foundation for proofs.
definitions.example: In arithmetic, 0 ≠ 1 is a simple truth that helps prove other things.

definitions.definition: A bigger number system where every equation has a solution, like adding imaginary numbers so that x² = -1 has an answer.
definitions.example: The complex numbers are the algebraic closure of the real numbers.

definitions.definition: When order breaks down and things become random or disconnected, like a crowd turning into chaos.
definitions.example: In quantum physics, decoherence is when a particle's wave-like behavior disappears because it interacts with its environment.

definitions.definition: A pair of opposite forces or directions, like the north and south ends of a magnet.
definitions.example: A battery has a positive and negative polarity.

definitions.definition: When two different things share the same underlying pattern, like a bird's wing and a fish's fin both being used for movement.
definitions.example: The bones in a human arm and a bat wing are structurally homologous.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that creates a whole series of numbers or patterns, like a seed that grows into a tree.
definitions.example: The Fibonacci sequence can be generated by a simple formula.

definitions.definition: Cannot be split into separate, independent parts, like a cake that can't be separated into flour and eggs after baking.
definitions.example: A non-factorable function means the whole is more than the sum of its parts.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven wrong by an experiment or observation, like a claim that can be tested.
definitions.example: The statement 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan disproves it.

definitions.definition: Based on real-world observation or experiment, not just theory.
definitions.example: A doctor's diagnosis is empirical when it's based on test results, not guesses.

definitions.definition: A pattern that a system tends to settle into over time, like a marble rolling to the bottom of a bowl.
definitions.example: A pendulum eventually stops at its lowest point, which is an attractor state.

definitions.definition: Computer models that show how a system changes over time, like a video game that simulates weather.
definitions.example: Scientists use dynamical simulations to predict how a hurricane will move.

definitions.definition: A main formula that describes how a whole system behaves, like the boss of all equations.
definitions.example: The master equation in this framework combines many variables into one big formula.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure how ordered or connected a system is, like a score for harmony.
definitions.example: A coherence function might give a high score to a well-organized team and a low score to a chaotic one.

definitions.definition: A serious promise or agreement that binds people together, like a marriage vow.
definitions.example: In the Bible, God made a covenant with Noah to never flood the earth again.

definitions.definition: When a quantum particle's many possible states suddenly become one definite state after being measured, like a spinning coin landing on heads or tails.
definitions.example: Before you look, a particle might be in many places at once; wavefunction collapse makes it pick one.

definitions.definition: The mystery of why and how we have subjective experiences, like feelings and awareness, not just brain activity.
definitions.example: Why does seeing red feel like something? That's the hard problem of consciousness.

definitions.definition: A big mismatch between the predicted and observed amount of dark energy in the universe, like a budget that's off by a trillion dollars.
definitions.example: The cosmological constant discrepancy is why scientists are puzzled about the universe's expansion rate.

definitions.definition: The study of how systems control themselves and communicate, like a thermostat that keeps a room at the right temperature.
definitions.example: Cybernetics looks at how feedback loops work in machines, animals, and societies.

definitions.definition: The study of what exists and what it means to be real, like asking 'is love as real as a rock?'
definitions.example: Ontology asks questions like 'do numbers exist?'

definitions.definition: The study of how we know things and what counts as knowledge, like asking 'how do you know that's true?'
definitions.example: Epistemology explores whether we can trust our senses or need proof.

definitions.definition: Something that could be different or might not exist at all, like the weather today.
definitions.example: Your choice of breakfast is contingent on what's in the fridge.

definitions.definition: Something that must be true and cannot be otherwise, like 2+2=4.
definitions.example: A necessary truth is one that holds in every possible world.

definitions.definition: A basic assumption that is accepted without proof, like a starting rule in a game.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation or being saved from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: Soteriology asks how people can be rescued from wrongdoing and find eternal life.

definitions.definition: The study of sin, wrongdoing, and moral failure.
definitions.example: Hamartiology explores what sin is and how it affects people.

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally pure over time.
definitions.example: Sanctification is like slowly becoming a better person through practice and help from God.

definitions.definition: Making up for a wrong or repairing a broken relationship, often through a sacrifice.
definitions.example: In Christianity, Jesus' death is seen as an atonement for humanity's sins.

definitions.definition: A theoretical field that represents the overall coherence or order in a system, like a force field for harmony.
definitions.example: The chi-field might be thought of as the 'glue' that holds things together in a meaningful way.

definitions.definition: The idea that moral values are built into the structure of reality, like a curved space that bends paths.
definitions.example: Moral curvature suggests that some actions naturally lead to better outcomes, like a slope that guides a ball downhill.

definitions.definition: A computer program that checks mathematical proofs for correctness, like a super-strict math teacher.
definitions.example: Lean 4 is used by mathematicians to make sure their proofs have no mistakes.

definitions.definition: Princeton Engineering Anomalies Research, a project that studied whether people's minds can affect random events.
definitions.example: PEAR experiments tested if focused attention could make a random number generator produce more ones than zeros.

definitions.definition: A large database of historical societies used to test theories about how civilizations evolve.
definitions.example: Seshat contains data on hundreds of ancient societies, like their size, government, and religion.

definitions.definition: A fake or false version of something that pretends to be the real thing.
definitions.example: In the proof, five impostor structures were tested and rejected because they didn't match the real pattern.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'what was to be shown,' used at the end of a proof to say 'done and proven.'
definitions.example: After solving a math problem, you might write QED to show it's finished.

definitions.definition: The property that order matters in an operation, like putting on socks then shoes vs. shoes then socks.
definitions.example: Matrix multiplication is non-commutative because A×B is not always equal to B×A.

definitions.definition: Having three parts or elements that form a pattern.
definitions.example: A triangle is a triadic shape because it has three sides.

definitions.definition: A set of elements with operations that follow specific rules, like numbers with addition and multiplication.
definitions.example: The integers with addition form an algebraic structure called a group.

definitions.definition: A proven step in a proof that eliminates fake or incorrect alternatives.
definitions.example: The impostor rejection lemma shows that five other possible structures don't work, leaving only the real one.

definitions.definition: A specific logical step showing that if grace could be undone, then a basic math contradiction would happen.
definitions.example: This step proves that grace is irreversible because reversing it would break math itself.

definitions.definition: A specific mathematical operation that combines two things to measure their joint order or harmony.
definitions.example: The coherence product might be like multiplying two signals to see how well they sync up.

definitions.definition: A special mathematical object used in the Theophysics framework, like a container for all the variables.
definitions.example: Ω might represent the whole universe of possible states in the model.

definitions.definition: A proof that shows order matters in the framework's operations.
definitions.example: The non-commutativity proof shows that doing A then B gives a different result than B then A.

definitions.definition: A proof that shows the framework has a three-part pattern.
definitions.example: The triadic structure proof demonstrates that the system naturally forms a trio of related parts.

definitions.definition: A proof that five alternative patterns are not valid.
definitions.example: This proof shows that five other possible structures don't fit the data, leaving only the correct one.

definitions.definition: A theorem stating that grace cannot be undone or reversed.
definitions.example: The grace_irreversible theorem says that once grace is given, it can't be taken back.
